headline: Week 5 Results Cheat Sheet
dek: Results recap for 20-26 April 2026. Week 5 stayed inside the Madrid ATP Masters 1000 event window, which runs 22 April - 3 May, 2026. With the week now complete from a fantasy standpoint, the focus shifts to who actually delivered, which profiles outperformed expectations, where lineups missed, and what the finished Madrid action means for future ATP Fantasy decisions.

columns.heading: What Paid Off
columns.body: The biggest fantasy wins came from players who paired advancement with Madrid-friendly scoring. In this format, the strongest returns usually come from names who not only moved through the draw, but also stacked clean wins, ace production, and stable match control in altitude clay conditions.
bullets: Advancement still drove the best overall fantasy outcomes.
Aggressive scorers gained extra value when wins came cleanly.
Players with stable early-round control were safer Bonus Ball outcomes.
Open sections mattered most when players actually converted them into multiple wins.

columns.heading: What Fell Short
columns.body: The misses were familiar: expensive names who failed to turn draw position into points, trendy values who could not survive their section, and volatile picks who looked attractive on paper but did not produce enough completed-week scoring.
bullets: Premium salaries hurt when they did not return multi-win value.
Popular sleeper picks were costly if they stalled early.
Dangerous sections punished lineups that chased ceiling over path security.
One-event slates left little room to recover from early exits.

cards.title: What Mattered In The Finished Week
paragraphs: ATP Fantasy still ran through the familiar 100-credit build with six starters, two alternates, and one Bonus Ball player scoring double. In a Madrid-only week, the completed results made one lesson clear: fantasy value came from converting opportunity into actual wins, not just landing in a promising section.

Madrid's altitude clay again rewarded players who could protect serve, play first-strike tennis, and keep scoreboard pressure on opponents. For fantasy managers, the best performers were the ones who combined progression with scoring efficiency, while many of the weaker returns came from picks that needed too many things to break right.
cards.subtitle: Results Edition Themes
bullets: Completed wins mattered more than pre-lock draw optimism.
Bonus Ball success depended on both ceiling and conversion.
Value picks worked best when they turned open paths into real points.
Misses often came from overrating theoretical upside.

items.body: Balanced builds were rewarded when they captured multiple players who actually advanced, rather than overcommitting to one fragile section or one expensive name.
Players with serve-driven or first-strike scoring profiles remained especially useful when they paired that style with match control and straight-sets potential.
Path analysis still mattered, but only when paired with realistic form and scoring fit. A good section alone was not enough.
If a pick depended on surviving several dangerous rounds just to justify salary, the downside was usually too high for a one-event fantasy slate.
The strongest premium returns came from top-end players who handled their early assignments cleanly and preserved deep-run equity through the week.
The best mid-range fantasy outcomes came from players who turned manageable sections into multiple wins and beat salary without needing a surprise title push.
The most useful picks were not just players who landed in favorable pockets, but the ones who actually capitalized on those openings with completed-week production.
The best Bonus Ball outcomes generally came from players with both advancement safety and enough scoring punch to separate from the field.
When a premium favorite had the cleanest route and converted it, that remained the most reliable multiplier approach.
A more aggressive Bonus Ball could work when a non-premium player found a genuinely open lane and turned it into several wins.
The biggest multiplier misses came from chasing volatility in dangerous sections where one early stumble erased double-score upside.
Players who emerged from softer sections and banked multiple wins were the clearest value successes of the week.
Serve-forward and first-strike profiles again proved useful when they translated conditions into aces, holds, and efficient wins.
Alternate-level names were most valuable when they offered real advancement equity rather than just low-cost exposure.
Cheap picks only helped when they produced actual points. The best bargains were the ones who gave lineups flexibility without sacrificing win potential.
Even strong names became weak fantasy investments when difficult sections prevented them from delivering enough completed-week value.
Some popular lower-cost plays looked attractive after the draw but failed to back it up with wins or scoring volume.
Traditional clay comfort alone was not enough in Madrid if the player profile lacked ace upside, straight-set potential, or realistic advancement.
Lineups that stacked exposure in one fragile pocket often lost too much equity when that part of the draw broke the wrong way.
